extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students studying representation theory (readers of Evan Chen's Napkin)
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter material and worked examples on finite-dimensional representations of algebras and groups: direct sums, irreducible/indecomposable representations, morphisms (intertwiners), Schur's lemma, representations of Mat_d(k), semisimple algebras, Maschke's theorem, characters and orthogonality. Includes definitions, propositions, proofs, and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular representation (Reg(A))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any k-algebra A is a representation (A, ρ) over itself, with a · b = ρ(a)(b) = ab (i.e. multiplication given by A). This is called the regular representation, denoted Reg(A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout as the algebra acting on itself; plays a central role in density arguments and in identifying intertwining operators Reg(A) → Reg(A) with right-multiplication by elements of A (Problem 19D⋆).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct sum of representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 19.3.1: If V = (V, ρV) and W = (W, ρW) are representations of A, then V ⊕ W is a representation with action a · (v,w) = (a · v, a · w).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct sums let you build block-diagonal actions (ρ(a) = diag(ρV(a), ρW(a))). Examples: stacking two copies of a 2-d representation to get a 4-d representation; used to decompose representations and to view Reg(A) images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representations of A ⊕ B decompose as VA ⊕ VB
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 19.3.5: Let A and B be k-algebras. Then every representation of A ⊕ B is of the form VA ⊕ VB where VA and VB are representations of A and B respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One cannot 'mix' the A and B actions; components act only on their corresponding subrepresentations. Proof uses projection by ρ(1A) and ρ(1B) and shows VA and VB are disjoint subrepresentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subrepresentation (invariant subspace)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 19.4.1: A subrepresentation W ⊆ V is a subspace W such that for any a ∈ A and w ∈ W, a · w ∈ W (equivalently, W is invariant under the action of A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If V = W1 ⊕ W2 as representations then each Wi is a subrepresentation. Many exercises ask to check invariance to test subrepresentation status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreducible and indecomposable representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 19.4.2: V is irreducible if it has no proper nonzero subrepresentations. V is indecomposable if there is no pair of proper subrepresentations W1, W2 with V = W1 ⊕ W2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irreducible implies indecomposable, but not conversely (example: certain R[x]-actions on R^2). Use irreducibles as 'atomic' building blocks; indecomposable is a weaker notion to flag pathological reducible-but-not-direct-sum cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexample: reducible but indecomposable
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise 19.4.5: A = R[x], V = R^2 with ρ(x) = [[1,0],[1,1]]; the only subrepresentation is W = {(t,0)} so V is reducible but not decomposable as a direct sum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: existence of such examples motivates the definition of 'completely reducible' and 'semisimple' to avoid this pathology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphisms / Intertwining operators
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 19.5.1: An intertwining operator T: V → W between representations (V, ρV) and (W, ρW) is a linear map satisfying T(a · v) = a · T(v) for all a ∈ A, v ∈ V. If T is invertible then it is an isomorphism of representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent to commutation of diagrams ρW(a) ◦ T = T ◦ ρV(a) for all a. Intertwiners are the morphisms in the category of A-representations (natural transformations viewpoint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic examples of intertwining operators
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples 19.5.4: (a) scalar maps T(v)=λv are intertwining; (b) inclusion of a subrepresentation is intertwining; (c) projection V1 ⊕ V2 ↠ V1 is intertwining; (d) commuting linear maps (rotations) give intertwiners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples show common sources of intertwiners; they also highlight when an isomorphism of vector spaces is not an isomorphism of representations (see non-example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-example: zero intertwiners between non-isomorphic irreps
rubrics_metrics.description: Example 19.5.5: For A = Mat2(R) ⊕ Mat2(R) acting on R^4 with block structure, the two obvious 2-d summands are isomorphic as vector spaces but not as representations, so any intertwiner between them is zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates that Homspace can be trivial when representations come from different components; important for later Hom decomposition results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kernel and image of an intertwiner are subrepresentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise 19.5.6: For T: V → W an intertwining operator, ker T ⊆ V and im T ⊆ W are subrepresentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This property is used in the proof of Schur's lemma and to deduce injectivity/surjectivity consequences from nonzero intertwiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schur’s lemma (basic form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 19.5.7: Let T: V → W be a nonzero intertwining operator. (a) If V is irreducible then T is injective. (b) If W is irreducible then T is surjective. In particular, if both are irreducible then T is an isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate consequences: Homrep between distinct irreps is either 0 or consists of isomorphisms. Used heavily to classify Hom spaces and to prove uniqueness properties of irreps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schur’s lemma over algebraically closed fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 19.5.8: Let k be algebraically closed and V a finite-dimensional irrep of A. Then any intertwining operator T: V → V is multiplication by a scalar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses eigenvalue argument: T has eigenvalue λ so T − λ id has zero kernel and thus is zero by Schur. Note failure over non-algebraically-closed fields (counterexample: rotation by 90° over R).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of representations of Mat_d(k)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 19.6.1: Let W = k^d be the obvious representation of A = Mat_d(k). Then every finite-dimensional representation of Mat_d(k) is isomorphic to W^{⊕n} for some n. In particular, W is irreducible (n=1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to finding linear maps Mi = ρ(Ei) satisfying the same multiplication table as matrix units. Typical argument shows V decomposes into images of idempotents (W1 ⊕ W2 etc.) and each summand is isomorphic to W.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decomposition via idempotent images (Mi images)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim 19.6.2 and 19.6.3: For Mat2(k) example, letting Wi = Im(Mi) yields V = W1 ⊕ W2 and W1 ≅ W2 (via M4 and M3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The construction of these image subspaces and maps between them constructs explicit copies of the standard representation and shows every representation is a direct sum of copies of it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completely reducible and semisimple definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: §20: A finite-dimensional representation is completely reducible if it can be written as a direct sum of irreducibles (i.e., no indecomposable reducible pathologies). A finite-dimensional algebra A is semisimple if all its finite-dimensional representations are completely reducible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation: avoid indecomposable-but-reducible representations like the R[x] example. Semisimplicity ensures representation theory reduces to classifying irreps and then assembling direct sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schur’s lemma for completely reducible representations (Hom decomposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 20.1.2: If V = ⊕_i V_i^{⊕n_i} and W = ⊕_i V_i^{⊕m_i} (Vi pairwise nonisomorphic irreps), then Homrep(V,W) ≅ ⊕_i Mat_{m_i×n_i}(k); an intertwining operator amounts to, for each i, an m_i×n_i matrix of scalars giving maps V_i^{⊕n_i} → V_i^{⊕m_i}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives explicit structure of Hom spaces as block-diagonal matrices per isomorphism class of irreps; non-isomorphic irreps don't 'talk to each other'. Used to count dimensions of Hom spaces and to analyze subrepresentation inclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subrepresentations of completely reducible representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary 20.1.3: If V = ⊕_i V_i^{⊕n_i} is completely reducible, any subrepresentation W is isomorphic to ⊕_i V_i^{⊕m_i} with m_i ≤ n_i, and the inclusion corresponds to matrices (for each i) of size n_i×m_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for understanding possible subrepresentations and their multiplicities when decomposing completely reducible modules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jacobson density theorem (density principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 20.2.1: For pairwise nonisomorphic finite-dimensional irreps (V1,…,Vr) of A, the map ⊕_i ρ_i : A ↠ ⊕_i Mat(V_i) is surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: given prescribed actions on each nonisomorphic irrep one can find a single element of A inducing those actions simultaneously (analogue of Chinese remainder theorem). Critical to show finiteness and independence statements about characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness bound for number of irreps
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary 20.2.2: Any finite-dimensional algebra A has at most dim A irreps, since sum_i (dim Vi)^2 ≤ dim A (coming from surjectivity to ⊕ Mat(Vi)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a numerical constraint on irreps; equality holds when A is semisimple (see sum-of-squares formula).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalences characterizing semisimple algebras
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 20.3.2: For finite-dimensional algebra A the following are equivalent: (i) A ≅ ⊕_i Mat_{d_i}(k) for some d_i; (ii) A is semisimple; (iii) Reg(A) is completely reducible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: use structure of Reg(A) and identification Homrep(Reg(A),Reg(A)) ≅ A^op to deduce matrix algebra decomposition when Reg(A) is completely reducible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maschke’s theorem (group algebras are semisimple)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 20.4.1: Let G be a finite group and k an algebraically closed field whose characteristic does not divide |G|. Then k[G] is semisimple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof method: given subrepresentation W ⊆ V, pick any projection π: V → W and average P = (1/|G|) Σ_{g∈G} ρ(g^{-1}) ◦ π ◦ ρ(g). P is an intertwining idempotent with im P = W and ker P its complement, giving V = W ⊕ ker P. Alternate proof over C uses averaging an inner product to make an invariant inner product and take orthogonal complements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters: definition and additivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 21.1.1: For finite-dimensional representation V = (V, ρ), the character χ_V : A → k is χ_V(a) = Tr(ρ(a)). It is k-linear and satisfies χ_{V⊕W} = χ_V + χ_W.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In group algebra case A = k[G], the character is the function G → k given by traces on group elements; characters encode much of the representation and are constant on conjugacy classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters factor through abelianization Aab
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 21.2.2 and surrounding text: The commutator subspace [A,A] is spanned by xy−yx, and every character vanishes on [A,A]. The abelianization A_ab := A/[A,A] is the target for characters; characters correspond to linear functionals on A_ab.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for A = k[G], A_ab corresponds to the space spanned by conjugacy classes, so characters are class functions. This explains why character values depend only on conjugacy classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear independence and spanning properties of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 21.2.5: (a) Characters of pairwise non-isomorphic finite-dimensional irreps are linearly independent in (A_ab)^∨. (b) If A is finite-dimensional and semisimple, the characters attached to irreps form a basis of (A_ab)^∨; in particular, number of irreps = dim A_ab.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (a) follows from the density theorem; part (b) uses that each matrix component Mat(Vi) has 1-dimensional abelianization. This yields the count of irreps equalling the number of conjugacy classes in group case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character trace identities: direct sum, tensor, dual
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 21.3.9: For representations V,W and g ∈ G: (a) χ_{V⊕W}(g) = χ_V(g) + χ_W(g). (b) χ_{V⊗W}(g) = χ_V(g) · χ_W(g). (c) χ_{V^∨}(g) = χ_V(g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (c) for finite groups over C uses eigenvalues which are roots of unity so λ^{-1} = conjugate equals λ and traces match. Care: these identities do not extend linearly to the whole group algebra C[G] in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthogonality of characters and inner product formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 21.3.4: For finite-dimensional complex representations V and W of G, ⟨χ_V, χ_W⟩ = dim Homrep(W, V), where ⟨f1,f2⟩ = (1/|G|) Σ_{g∈G} f1(g) f2(g). In particular, for irreps ⟨χ_V, χ_W⟩ = 1 if V ≅ W and 0 otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses χ_V(g) χ_W(g) = χ_{V ⊗ W^∨}(g) and averages the projector (1/|G|) Σ_g g to count fixed points in V ⊗ W^∨, which correspond to intertwining maps via V ⊗ W^∨ ≅ Hom(W,V). Consequence: irreducible characters form an orthonormal basis of class functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tensor product and dual representation definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions 21.3.6–21.3.7: Dual V^∨ has action (g·ξ)(v) = ξ(ρ(g^{-1})(v)). Tensor product V ⊗ W has action g·(v⊗w) = (ρ_V(g)v) ⊗ (ρ_W(g)w).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These constructions are used to convert products of character values into single characters (χ_{V⊗W} = χ_V χ_W) and to identify Hom spaces with invariant subspaces of tensor products.
